title: Age-related changes in 100-km ultra-marathon running performance
authors: Knechtle B, Rust CA, Rosemann T, Lepers R
population: Finishers of the 100 km Lauf Biel (Switzerland), 1998-2010, both sexes
findings: The best 100-km times were observed at ages 30-49 for males and 30-54 for females.
Mean age of the top ten finishers increased by 0.4 years per annum for both sexes (males P = 0.003; females P = 0.02).
Age-related decline in running performance was similar between sexes until 60-64 years and greater for females after 65.
The share of finishers rose for the 40-49 and 50-59 age groups and fell for the 18-29 and 30-39 groups over the period.
limitations: Single race, finishers only (survivor bias), cross-sectional by age, no physiological or training data; abstract gives no sample size.
implications: For 100 km goals, best times were observed in age 30-49 (men) and 30-54 (women), so applying an age-related target decline before about 50 is not supported by this data; the researcher's claim that ultras 'peak later than middle-distance' is not tested in this abstract.
After the best-age window, apply the general decline model; the sex difference appears only after 65.

verification.notes: Crossref (online 2011) and Europe PMC (print 2012) match; findings confirmed. Implication softened: comparison with shorter distances is not in the abstract.
